prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Why hast thou nothing in thy face? Thou idol of the human race, Thou tyrant of the human heart, The flower of lovely youth that art; Yea, and that standest in thy youth An image of eternal Truth, With thy exuberant flesh so fair, That only Pheidias might compare, Ere from his chaste marmoreal form Time had decayed the colours warm; Like to his gods in thy proud dress, Thy starry sheen of nakedness. Surely thy body is thy mind, For in thy face is nought to find, Only thy soft unchristen’d smile, That shadows neither love nor guile, But shameless will and power immense, In secret sensuous innocence. O king of joy, what is thy thought? I dream thou knowest it is nought, And wouldst in darkness come, but thou Makest the light where’er thou go. Ah yet no victim of thy grace, None who e’er long’d for thy embrace, Hath cared to look upon thy face.

Keywords: Why, Thou, The

outputs.L1:
Why hast thou nothing in thy face,  
Thou idol of the human race,  
Thou tyrant of the human heart,  
The flower of lovely youth thou art?  
Yea, thou who standest in thy youth  
An image of eternal Truth,  
With flesh exuberant and fair,  
That only Pheidias might compare,  
Ere Time, from his chaste marmoreal form,  
Had faded all the colours warm;  
Like to his gods in thy proud dress—  
Thy starry sheen of nakedness.

Surely thy body is thy mind,  
For in thy face is nought to find  
Save thy soft, unchristened smile,  
That shadows neither love nor guile,  
But shameless will and power immense  
In secret, sensuous innocence.

O king of joy, what is thy thought?  
I dream thou knowest it is nought,  
And wouldst come cloaked in darkness—but thou  
Makest light wherever thou dost go.  
Ah, yet no victim of thy grace,  
None who e’er longed for thine embrace,  
Hath cared to look upon thy face.
outputs.L2:
Why does your countenance reveal nothing? You are humanity’s adored image, ruler of every heart, and the finest blossom of beautiful youth. In your young form, you stand as a likeness of everlasting Truth. Your abundant flesh is so flawless that only a statue by Pheidias could rival it—before time faded the warm colors once painted upon his pure marble figures. In your majestic nakedness, glittering like stars, you resemble one of his gods.

Your body itself must contain your mind, since your features disclose no inner life. They show only a gentle, unbaptized smile that suggests neither affection nor deceit, but instead a vast, unashamed force of will, joined mysteriously with innocent sensuality.

O sovereign of delight, what occupies your thoughts? I imagine you know that the answer is nothing. Perhaps you would approach under cover of darkness, yet wherever you appear, you create light. Even so, none of those conquered by your beauty—none who have desired your embrace—has ever cared to study your face.
outputs.L3:
The speaker addresses a beautiful young man as though he were an idol, a figure with almost divine power over human desire and affection. His beauty makes him the object of universal longing, allowing him to dominate the emotions of those around him. The youth’s body is likened to the idealized, godlike sculptures of the ancient Greek artist Pheidias. Through this comparison, his physical form becomes more than merely attractive: it appears perfect, timeless, and expressive of an eternal truth.

Yet his face seems strangely detached from any recognizable inner life. It reveals no clear thought, passion, or emotion, displaying only a gentle and enigmatic smile. This smile cannot be interpreted as either loving or deceptive; instead, it preserves the youth’s mystery and emotional distance. Although his inner self remains inaccessible, he radiates immense will, sensual innocence, and an intense joy that seems to illuminate every place he enters.

Those who fall under the spell of his beauty long above all for physical closeness and the pleasure of his embrace. Their fascination is directed less toward his face, thoughts, or personality than toward the grace and perfection of his body. In this way, the youth is admired not as a complete individual but as an idealized physical presence—an embodiment of beauty, desire, vitality, and unattainable perfection.
outputs.L4:
The poem takes the form of a direct apostrophe to an extraordinarily beautiful young man. From the outset, the speaker is captivated by his physical appearance, describing him less as an ordinary human being than as an idealized work of art. His body appears radiant, perfectly formed, and almost sculptural, as though it belonged to a classical statue rather than to a living person. This emphasis elevates the youth into an object of aesthetic and sensual admiration while simultaneously creating a sense of distance between him and the speaker.

Yet the perfection of the young man’s body is sharply contrasted with the apparent emptiness of his face. Although his outward form suggests vitality and power, his expression seems to reveal little thought, emotion, or individuality. The speaker searches for signs of an inner life but finds only a beautiful surface. In this way, the poem introduces an unsettling tension: the youth appears intensely present as a physical being but absent as a conscious person. His beauty makes him visible, yet it also prevents him from being fully known.

The poem’s imagery contributes to this dehumanization. By comparing the youth to a sculpture or ideal form, the speaker turns him into something to be looked at and desired rather than understood. His body becomes an object onto which the observer projects fantasies of perfection. What might ordinarily be considered a limitation—the lack of intellectual or emotional depth—does not weaken his attraction. Instead, it may even intensify it, because the absence of a clearly expressed personality allows desire to dominate the encounter.

By the conclusion, sensual beauty has eclipsed every other aspect of the young man’s identity. His commanding physical presence proves more powerful than any question about what he thinks or feels. The speaker recognizes, implicitly or explicitly, that desire can reduce another person to an image, a body, or an object of possession. The poem therefore celebrates physical beauty while also exposing its troubling power. The youth is irresistible precisely because he has been transformed into a perfect surface, but that transformation comes at the cost of his humanity. Ultimately, the poem reveals how desire can both glorify and erase its object, making the beloved seem almost divine while denying him a complex inner life.
outputs.L5:
### Why, Thou, The

Why does the moon pursue the restless sea,  
while stars keep watch in silent symmetry?  
Thou wanderer beneath the fading sky,  
hast carried countless questions passing by.

The road is long, the destination veiled,  
yet every heart moves on where hope has failed.  
Why seek an answer carved in stone,  
when thou canst make the unknown road thine own?

The world is not a riddle to complete,  
but wind and dust beneath uncertain feet.  
So ask not only why the shadows fall—  
thou art the light that gives a shape to all.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem in archaic English praising the physical beauty of a proud, statuesque young man whose face reveals no inner thought or emotion.
counterfactuals.output:
Behold him stand, as carven from the stone,  
A youth full proud, in noble stature set;  
His brow a throne where silence reigns alone,  
His lips with neither mirth nor sorrow met.  

His cheek hath ta’en the dawn’s unblemish’d hue,  
His hair the raven’s dark and glossy wing;  
His shoulders broad, his limbs of comely thew,  
As though Apollo walk’d in mortal spring.  

Yet in his gaze no secret light doth stir,  
Nor tender thought beneath his visage move;  
No wrath may mar, no gentler dream confer  
The faintest sign of hatred or of love.  

O beauteous mask, O marble-hearted grace,  
Proud as a god, and silent as his face.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a decadent Victorian-style poem comparing a beautiful nude youth to one of Pheidias’s painted marble gods.
counterfactuals.output:
Before the porphyry dusk, a young man stood,  
Full-grown, yet touched with April’s golden breath;  
No veil profaned his body’s quiet good,  
So fair it mocked the solemn pride of Death.

He seemed some god from Pheidias’ dreaming hand,  
Not pallid as the marbles mourn to be,  
But stained with cinnabar, with brows gold-spanned,  
And lips like coral warmed by Attic sea.

The lamplight, jealous, lingered at his thigh;  
Soft shadow clasped the hollow of his side;  
A violet darkness slept beneath each eye,  
Where mortal languor warred with heavenly pride.

O painted god, from ruined temples flown,  
What priest could crown thee, what white victim bleed?  
My heart alone shall be thy altar-stone,  
My secret sigh the incense of thy creed.

Yet dawn came cold—the splendid vision stirred,  
And all Olympus faded from the room;  
He smiled, and with that frail, unguarded word,  
Made flesh more deathless than the sculptor’s bloom.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a lyrical meditation on a handsome youth whose body seems to be his entire mind, blending sensual attraction, classical imagery, and unease at his emotional emptiness.
counterfactuals.output:
He stood in the doorway like a young god misplaced among ordinary furniture—an adult in the first blaze of manhood, all bronze shoulder and quiet mouth, the clean architecture of his body seeming less inhabited than displayed. Looking at him, one thought of marble warmed by afternoon: Apollo stepping down from the pediment, not to prophesy, but merely to be seen.

His skin appeared to know everything his eyes did not. Each movement carried its own lucid intelligence—the flex of a hand, the long turn of the neck, the easy balance of hip and heel. Desire gathered around him as light gathers on a statue, discovering every plane. To watch him breathe was to believe, briefly, that breath itself might be wisdom.

Yet when he spoke, the words fell without roots. Nothing trembled behind them. Praise entered him and vanished, as coins vanish into a deep, dry fountain. Sorrow approached and found no door. Even tenderness, laying its palm against his chest, seemed to touch only the beautiful wall of him.

Perhaps Narcissus was not ruined by loving his reflection, but by finding there was no one beneath it. Perhaps the gods, jealous of perfection, had hollowed this young man gently, leaving the radiant shell: thighs shaped for the games, lips fit for wine and vows, eyes as calm as a sea that has never carried a ship.

I wanted him with the old, helpless hunger—with the worshipper’s longing to press mortal warmth against sacred stone. But unease moved within desire like a snake in laurel. What could embrace mean to a body that was also its own soul? What answer could come from flesh so eloquent it had never needed to learn the language of the heart?

He smiled, and the room brightened.

He smiled, and no one was there.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write 28 rhyming lines addressed to an irresistibly beautiful but inscrutable young man, using words such as “thou,” “hast,” and “wouldst” and evoking pagan sculpture, nakedness, power, and desire.
counterfactuals.output:
O thou, whose beauty puts the dawn to shame,  
Thou hast Apollo’s brow, Ares’ flame.  
From pagan marble did the gods devise  
That naked grace, those dark, unanswering eyes.  

No sculptor’s hand could shape so proud a breast,  
Nor teach such power in perfect limbs to rest.  
Wouldst thou but speak, the listening stars would fall,  
Yet silence girds thee like a temple wall.  

Thy smile is wine from Dionysus’ vine,  
One drop, and all my mortal thoughts are thine.  
Thou standest bare as some immortal youth,  
A form divine that veils a secret truth.  

Cold as the stone, yet burning as the sun,  
Thou makest conquest ere the war’s begun.  
What hidden kingdom hast thou locked within,  
Behind that brow untouched by grief or sin?  

I seek thy soul, but find a mask of gold;  
I seek thy heart, but meet a riddle cold.  
Still would I kneel where thy white footsteps move,  
A slave to wonder and a king in love.  

Thy nakedness hath more than armor’s might;  
It wounds by day and haunts the dreaming night.  
O beautiful, inscrutable, and proud,  
Thou art the lightning sleeping in the cloud.  

If thou wouldst yield one whisper of desire,  
My blood would rise like incense into fire.  
Yet though thy mystery denies me bliss,  
I worship still—and burn for what it is.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
